extracted.intended_audience: teachers, teacher-educators, and educational researchers interested in formative assessment and classroom feedback
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing and delivering formative feedback and classroom discourse to improve student learning, rooted in self-regulated learning (SRL), cognitive-acceleration, and dynamic-assessment perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic and prognostic decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers must both diagnose what a student response reveals about the student's thinking/motivation and then choose (prognose) an optimum contingent response, often under severe time constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are two distinct steps: rapid interpretation of student contributions (diagnostic) and choosing the best immediate action (prognostic). Decisions are complex, often made in seconds, and may require choosing among pointing out flaws, opening exploratory discussion, or working on student resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make learner self-assessment overt
rubrics_metrics.description: Learners inevitably deploy self-assessment before any outcome; effective practice makes that self-assessment explicit to support improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The role of the teacher is not to initiate self-assessment but to render it more overt (e.g., prompt students to articulate criteria they used) so it can serve as a step to improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify source(s) of student error or partial success
rubrics_metrics.description: When an output is imperfect, teachers should entertain multiple possible causes (language misunderstanding, wrong purpose/context assumptions, misleading superficial cues, task misunderstanding, ineffective strategy, misunderstanding quality criteria, or shallow-level responses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a checklist of plausible explanations (examples in text) rather than assuming a single cause; this widens the range of appropriate feedback responses and avoids misinterpretation (e.g., mislabeling resourceful responses as misbehaviour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Link feedback to multiple SRL elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback should not only address task interpretation but may need to be linked with the learner's understanding of quality criteria, strategy choice, and self-regulation processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis may require combined feedback: e.g., correct a task misunderstanding while also addressing the student's criteria for judging quality or coaching strategy selection and monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task-level feedback (Hattie & Temperley)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback that focuses on faults in the interpretation of the task or in the outcome produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-analyses show high effect sizes when students receive information about the task and how to perform it more effectively. Use to correct misunderstandings about what the task requires or about errors in a produced product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-level feedback (Hattie & Temperley)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback focused on the main processes needed to understand or perform a task; serves as advance-organiser to cue better strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Should connect with learners' own error-detection strategies and cue more effective approaches. Useful for moving students from inefficient to more effective procedural or conceptual strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-regulation-level feedback (Hattie & Temperley)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback aimed at self-monitoring, directing, and regulating one’s actions (i.e., meta-cognitive and volitional processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps students plan, monitor, and evaluate their own work. Effectiveness depends on learners' willingness to engage and their confidence in their own productions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal/affective feedback (Hattie & Temperley)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback that concerns personal evaluations — praise, judgment, or affective messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These have weaker effects on learning if used alone; can enhance motivation for some learners, but unclear negative feedback can damage performance for students with low self-image. Be cautious about relying on praise/grades as primary feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid formative feedback that centers on grades/praise as the main message
rubrics_metrics.description: Focusing feedback on marks, grades, competition, or evaluative judgment can inhibit attention to substantive advice and promote performance/ego orientations rather than task-orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research (Butler; Dweck) shows such feedback can damage learning orientation. Where possible, separate evaluative judgement from advice for improvement and prioritize actionable guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor feedback to learner confidence and transaction costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Effectiveness of feedback depends on learners' confidence and the 'transaction costs' of engaging with the feedback; high confidence supports engagement, low confidence may lead to ignoring feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unclear negative feedback for students with uncertain self-image; scaffold feedback to reduce transaction costs and encourage help-seeking rather than answer-seeking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design tasks to create cognitive conflict, foster metacognition, and enable social construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective formative programmes (e.g., Cognitive Acceleration) design tasks to generate cognitive conflict, prompt reflection on thinking, and require dialogue so ideas move from social to internal planes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tasks that challenge cognitive operations (seriation, causality, classification, proportionality, probability), include 'bridging' activities to connect contexts, and allocate dedicated time for such tasks (e.g., one period every two weeks in CASE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted, sequenced tasks and coherent programme design
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs that produce lasting benefits use a closely specified set of activities, a coherent sequence of reasoning tasks, and prescribed pedagogic practices supported by teacher training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained coherent sequences and explicit aims help teachers anticipate student reactions and narrow appropriate responses, improving implementation fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit the learner’s Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) with sustained follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers should not only resolve immediate obstacles but strategically follow up successes to build learners' capacity, exploiting the learner’s ZPD even if it temporarily diverts from curriculum pace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dynamic assessment emphasizes sustained, strategic interventions that develop learning capacity rather than quick fixes for one task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain explicit learning intentions and teacher responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers should have (implicit or explicit) learning intentions and engineer learning environments that balance student needs with accountability to disciplinary standards; not abdicating responsibility to 'chair' discussions without guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning intentions need not be narrow or identical for all students but should guide task selection and feedback. Engineering must maximize opportunities for autonomy while ensuring disciplinary content is enacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contingent assessment planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers should limit their teaching plan so interactions stay within a range they can foresee and prepare for, enabling more effective contingent feedback responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focused programmes and professional development simplify contingent planning because they narrow the range of appropriate responses and allow anticipation of typical student reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the appropriate balance of classroom discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Class discussion should be located between monologue and free-flowing chat; the optimal point along this spectrum will vary by subject and aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formative assessment cannot flourish at the extremes; teachers must decide how strongly to steer discussion versus allowing open social talk depending on discipline and goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elicit reasoned contributions and delay teacher judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage pupil contributions in full sentences showing reasoning (use of 'think', 'because'), collect multiple contributions, summarise, compare differences, and postpone the teacher's own verdict until many have contributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice increases the proportion of substantive student talk, reduces rejection feelings, and helps steer the class to collective learning rather than addressing individual answers alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote pupils as instructional resources for one another
rubrics_metrics.description: Use peer dialogue and peer-assessment as part of formative practice, with the teacher modelling appropriate peer interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer-assessment requires modelling and scaffolding; written feedback can set up one-to-one dialogues that are simpler to manage than whole-class interaction because teachers have time to craft responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise limits of the teacher’s model of student thinking (principle of fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any model the teacher constructs of a child's conceptualisations is built from the teacher's own conceptual elements; aim for models that are viable within available experience rather than assuming a match with the child's inner thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be humble in interpretation, acknowledge uncertainty, and be willing to ask for further explanation rather than immediately labelling responses as wrong or misbehaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align feedback strategy with overarching learning aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether priority is subject-specific aims or improving general learning capacity; this decision will affect the nature of formative interactions and what feedback emphasises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs that prioritise learning capacity (CA, DA) will adopt tasks and feedback aimed at developing reasoning processes, possibly at the expense of short-term curriculum coverage; subject-priority lessons will embed formative practices within disciplinary aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tune tasks to student responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers must adjust (tune) tasks as responses occur to maintain engagement and progress towards intended learning outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tuning is challenging and context-dependent; guidance exists (e.g., Dillon) on strategies to adjust tasks on-the-fly. Poor tuning can cause missed opportunities to draw students into productive learning trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target cognitive operations explicitly in task design
rubrics_metrics.description: Design tasks that deliberately challenge key cognitive operations (e.g., seriation, causality, classification, proportionality, probability) when aiming to develop reasoning skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly incorporating such schemas in task design supports metacognition and transfer; include bridging activities to help students recognise where similar reasoning applies elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider reverse feedback (student-to-teacher)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feedback is not only teacher-to-student; attention should be given to student feedback to teachers as part of formative practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The literature reviewed gives little direct attention to this, but practitioners should be mindful of and solicit student perspectives to inform teaching choices and the teacher’s own learning.
